questions.q: Describe a city you visited and would like to visit again
questions.answer:
Last spring I spent a weekend in Samarkand with my family, and it is the city I would most like to revisit. I had seen photographs of its famous squares, but photographs had not prepared me for the atmosphere of the place. We arrived early, left our bags at a small guesthouse and went straight out to explore.

What struck me first was the contrast between its historic buildings and the ordinary life going on around them. At Registan Square, I found myself **taking in the architecture** rather than rushing to take pictures. Later, we **wandered through the streets**, stopped for tea and **tried the local food**. An elderly shopkeeper told us a little about the neighbourhood, and that **brief conversation** made the trip feel much more personal. By the time the sun went down, I had completely lost track of time.

If I returned, I would **set aside more time** for the smaller places I missed. On our first visit we had tried to **fit too much into one day**, so I would travel at a slower pace and perhaps visit a museum. What makes the city memorable is that it offers both a **sense of history** and a **lively atmosphere**. It also gave me the chance to **spend quality time** with my family. Even now, a photograph of that afternoon can **bring back vivid memories**.

On a second visit I would ask local people which ordinary places they enjoy, not just follow a list of landmarks. I might discover a neighbourhood café or a quiet street that I missed completely the first time. That would let me understand the city as more than a collection of beautiful buildings.

questions.q: Describe a toy you enjoyed playing with in your childhood
questions.answer:
One childhood toy I remember especially well was a small box of building blocks. It wasn't an expensive set, but it gave me an extraordinary amount of entertainment. My parents had bought it for me when I was quite young, and I kept it for years, even after some pieces had gone missing.

I would spread the blocks across the floor and **build miniature houses** or bridges for my toy cars. The fun lay in the fact that there was no single correct result. If a tower collapsed, I could **start from scratch** and come up with a better design. Sometimes a friend would join me, and we would **make up stories** about the people living in our imaginary town. We usually **lost track of time** until someone called us for dinner.

Looking back, that simple toy did more than **keep me entertained**. It encouraged me to **use my imagination** and **solve small problems** without worrying about failure. Having built something with my own hands, I felt a genuine **sense of achievement**, even if the structure fell apart ten minutes later. I had other toys, of course, but the blocks **stood out in my memory** because I could change the game every day. They remind me that children often need the **freedom to experiment** more than they need a complicated toy.

I still think about that toy when I see a child being given something with dozens of instructions. The simplest pieces allowed us to invent our own rules. Had I received a completed model instead, I doubt I would remember it as clearly today.

questions.q: Describe a film you enjoyed watching
questions.answer:
The film I'd like to talk about is *The Martian*, which I watched at home one evening after a friend had recommended it. It's a fictional story about an astronaut who is accidentally left on Mars and has to survive until a rescue becomes possible. I expected an ordinary space adventure, but the film turned out to be much more engaging than that.

What held my attention was the way the main character **tackled one problem at a time**. Instead of giving up, he tried to **make the most of limited resources**, often with a surprisingly good sense of humour. The story also showed people on Earth **working towards a common goal**, even when they disagreed about the safest approach. Although I knew the plot was invented, the setbacks felt real enough to **keep me on the edge of my seat**. I was particularly impressed by the moments when a tiny calculation could have enormous consequences.

I enjoyed the film because it **struck a balance** between suspense, science and human warmth. It didn't pretend that determination alone could solve everything: the astronaut needed both his own skills and help from others. After the credits, I found myself **thinking about resilience** and how important it is to **stay calm under pressure**. I would happily watch it again, partly for the **visual effects**, but mainly for its message that **creative thinking** becomes most valuable when plans go wrong.

My favourite scene is the point at which the astronaut has to rethink a plan that seemed perfectly sound. It shows how **a fresh approach** can matter as much as technical knowledge. That combination of intelligence, uncertainty and humour gave the story a human quality I hadn't expected from a film set so far from Earth.

questions.q: Describe a place you would recommend living in, other than your hometown
questions.answer:
I would recommend Samarkand as a place to live, at least for someone who enjoys history and doesn't mind a steady flow of visitors. I don't come from there, but I spent a few days in the city with my family. I realise a short visit cannot tell me everything about daily life, so this is a personal impression rather than a guarantee.

The first thing I noticed was how easy it was to **explore on foot** in the areas we visited. There were places to eat, small shops and spaces where people could **meet up with friends**. Its historic sites create a **distinctive character** that many newer places struggle to develop. At the same time, I saw families going about ordinary routines, which made it feel like a **lived-in city** rather than a museum. One evening, a local person gave us directions and then suggested a nearby place for tea; that **warm hospitality** stayed with me.

If I were thinking of moving there, I would first **look into the cost of living**, transport and study opportunities. Having said that, the city seems to offer a good **change of pace** for someone like me. I could imagine **settling into a routine** while still having interesting places to explore on weekends. For me, a good home is somewhere I can **feel at ease**, **build a community** and remain curious about my surroundings.

I would also tell someone considering a move to visit at an ordinary time, not only during a holiday. Seeing how people commute and buy groceries would provide a more honest picture. A recommendation is useful only when it includes practical questions alongside enthusiasm.

questions.q: Describe a quiet place you like to be alone or would like to visit
questions.answer:
There is a small park a short walk from my home where I like to spend time by myself. It isn't silent, but once I leave the main road, the traffic becomes a distant sound. There are a few benches under the trees, and I usually go there in the late afternoon when most people are on their way home.

On days when schoolwork starts to **pile up**, I take a book or just sit and **let my thoughts settle**. I sometimes **watch the light change** through the branches instead of looking at my phone. That sounds like a small thing, but it helps me **take a break from screens** and **clear my head**. Once, I had been struggling with an essay introduction for hours. After twenty minutes in the park, I returned home with a simpler idea that worked much better.

What I like most is that nobody expects me to do anything there. I can **enjoy my own company** without feeling lonely. If I had more time, I'd like to find a similar place in the countryside, with more trees and fewer cars. For now, though, this park is **within easy reach**, so I can visit it whenever I need to **slow down for a while**. It gives me a rare **sense of calm** in an otherwise busy week. That is why I keep going back rather than looking for a more impressive place.

Even when other people use the park, we tend to leave one another alone, which is part of its appeal. I do not need a perfectly empty space to feel peaceful. A place can still offer **a little privacy** if the people in it respect one another's quiet.

questions.q: Describe a piece of local news that interested many people
questions.answer:
One piece of local news that attracted attention where I live was an announcement about improving a busy neighbourhood road and the pedestrian crossing beside it. I heard about it first from relatives and then saw people discussing it in a local group. I can't recall every official detail, but the conversation around it was memorable.

That crossing is close to shops and a place where many students pass, so people had been **raising concerns** about traffic for some time. Some residents welcomed the proposed changes because they hoped it would **make the area safer**. Others were worried that construction might **disrupt daily travel** or affect nearby businesses. At home we talked about how even a modest road project can **have a direct impact** on families who use the route every day.

What made the story interesting to me was not the construction itself but the range of reactions. It reminded me that local news often **brings practical issues to light** that national headlines overlook. Ideally, officials would **listen to residents** and **keep people informed** as plans develop. I also learned to **check the original announcement** rather than rely on comments alone, because a rumour can spread quickly. Whether or not every suggestion is accepted, a public discussion gives people a chance to **voice their opinions** and perhaps improve the result.

I followed the story for a few days and noticed that the discussion became more specific once people had seen a proposed timetable. It reminded me to **distinguish facts from rumours** when a story affects my neighbourhood. What matters most is whether the eventual change actually helps the people who use that crossing.

questions.q: Describe an animal story or character
questions.answer:
The animal story that has stayed with me is *The Lion and the Mouse*. I first heard it as a child and later came across it in English while practising reading. It is short enough to retell in a minute, yet it has a point that is easy to remember.

In the story, a lion catches a mouse but decides to **let it go**. The mouse promises to help one day, which sounds absurd because the lion is so much bigger. Later, when the lion gets trapped in a net, the mouse **comes to the rescue** and gnaws through the ropes. The moment **turns the tables**: the creature that seemed powerless becomes the only one able to help. As a child I enjoyed the surprise. As I grew older, I began to notice how neatly the story **challenges assumptions** about strength and usefulness.

The mouse is my favourite character because it **keeps its promise** without making a grand speech. The lion also deserves credit for showing mercy before there is anything to gain from it. If I were telling this story to a younger child, I would keep the language simple and ask what they would have done in the lion's place. The lesson I take from it is to **treat others with respect** and not **judge by appearances**. Although the plot is simple, its message can **stay with you** for years and **apply to everyday life**.

It is also a useful story for language learning because the characters and sequence are so clear. I can retell it in simple English, then try to express its meaning in a more nuanced way. That has helped me **practise storytelling** while thinking about the lesson behind it.

If he makes a mistake, he doesn't become embarrassed; he asks for a correction and **makes a mental note**. He also **switches between languages** without translating every sentence word for word. Once, while we were preparing a short presentation, he explained a difficult idea in two different ways until everyone understood it. What impressed me wasn't his accent but his ability to **get his point across**.

Watching him has taught me that apparent ease can hide a great deal of practice. He listens regularly, **reviews useful phrases** and looks for chances to speak outside class. I have tried to **follow his example** by recording myself and asking more questions. If I could learn one thing from him, it would be his willingness to **take risks with language**. He rarely lets the fear of an imperfect sentence **hold him back**, and that attitude seems to help him **make rapid progress**.

I used to compare my progress with his and feel discouraged. Then I realised that I was seeing the result of habits he had built over a long time. Now I ask him how he practises rather than simply telling him he is talented; his methods are more useful to me than a compliment.

questions.q: Describe a place you found boring
questions.answer:
The place that comes to mind is a waiting area in an administrative building that I visited with a relative. I don't want to be unfair to the people working there; the building served a necessary purpose. From a visitor's point of view, however, it was an unusually dull place to spend an afternoon.

We had arrived early for an appointment, but the schedule was delayed and we ended up **waiting around** much longer than expected. The room had plain walls, rows of chairs and almost nothing to read. There was little **natural light**, and the slow movement of the queue made time seem to **drag on**. I tried to read on my phone, but the connection kept failing, so even that did not help. Eventually my relative and I **struck up a conversation** with another visitor, which at least made the experience feel less impersonal.

What made the place boring was less its appearance than the lack of information. Had we known how long the wait would be, we could have **made better use of our time**. A clear display, some seating near a window and regular updates would have **made a noticeable difference**. The experience taught me to **bring something to read** whenever I expect a queue. I also realised that a space can be **perfectly functional** yet still fail to **feel welcoming** or **hold your attention**.

I think about that visit whenever a place seems boring at first glance. Sometimes the surroundings are not the real problem; uncertainty and a lack of choice make the wait worse. Even a small notice telling visitors what to expect could have changed how we experienced that afternoon.

questions.q: Describe a successful business person you know
questions.answer:
I'd choose the owner of a small bookshop in my area. I know her as a customer rather than as a close friend, so I cannot speak about her finances. Still, she has kept the shop running for years, and the number of people who return suggests that she has built something valuable.

When I first visited, I expected a typical store where someone simply takes payment. Instead, she asked what I wanted to learn and **recommended a book** that suited my level. She seems to **understand her customers** and remembers what regular visitors enjoy reading. During a period when more people were buying online, she began posting short reviews and offering a way to reserve a title. It was a practical step that helped the shop **adapt to change** without losing its personal character. She also hosts occasional reading discussions, which **bring people together**.

What I admire is the way she appears to **build long-term trust** rather than chase a quick sale. A business needs to **cover its costs**, of course, but service and reputation matter as well. Seeing her work has changed my idea of success: it can mean **meeting a real need**, **creating a welcoming space** and earning enough to keep doing it. If I ever started a project of my own, I would try to **learn from her approach** and **pay attention to feedback**.

I am especially interested in how she chooses books for beginners. Recommending something too difficult might put a new reader off altogether, while a suitable first book could lead to years of reading. That judgement is a form of expertise that a photograph of a shop would never reveal.

questions.q: Describe an advertisement presented by a famous person
questions.answer:
An advertisement I remember featured a well-known athlete promoting sports shoes. I saw it online before a video, and although I cannot recall the brand, I remember the structure clearly. It showed the athlete practising early in the morning, making mistakes and gradually improving rather than simply posing with the product.

The advert tried to **catch the viewer's attention** with quick scenes and energetic music. The celebrity's presence helped the brand **make a strong impression**, but what interested me was the story of repeated practice. It suggested that the shoes belonged to a wider message about perseverance. That was **a clever marketing choice**, because people could remember the feeling even if they forgot the technical features. At the same time, I noticed that the advert said very little about comfort or durability, which are the things I would actually consider before buying shoes.

I didn't **rush out to buy** the product. Instead, I looked at a few reviews and **compared different options**. A famous face may **give a product visibility**, but it doesn't automatically **prove its quality**. Still, I think the advert worked as a piece of storytelling: it made an ordinary object seem connected to effort and progress. If I saw it again, I would probably **recognise it immediately**. It taught me to **separate the message from the facts** before I **make a purchase**.

The advert also made me more aware of how easily an inspiring story can transfer positive feelings to a product. That isn't necessarily dishonest, but it is different from evidence that the shoes suit my feet. I would rather try them on and ask practical questions before spending money.

questions.q: Describe someone who enjoys growing plants
questions.answer:
My aunt enjoys growing plants, and her small garden is the first thing I notice whenever I visit. She doesn't have a huge piece of land, but she uses every corner carefully. There are flowers near the gate and vegetables in the sunniest part of the garden.

She taught herself to **grow plants from seeds** by asking neighbours questions and learning from her own mistakes. Each morning she checks whether the soil is dry, **waters the plants** if necessary and removes weeds before they spread. Once I watched her move a young tomato plant because it wasn't **getting enough sunlight**. A week later it looked noticeably healthier. She explained that gardening involves observation as much as hard work, and that you cannot **force a plant to grow** faster simply by worrying about it.

What I admire is her patience. When a crop fails, she tries to **work out what went wrong** rather than abandon the whole garden. She sometimes **shares the harvest** with relatives, which makes her effort feel generous as well as practical. Visiting her has made me **pay closer attention** to the changing seasons and the work behind food on a plate. If I had a garden of my own, I would **start with a few herbs** and ask her advice. She has shown me that a small space can **bring real satisfaction** when you **take care of it consistently**.

One afternoon she let me help her prepare the soil. I discovered that even a small bed took more work than it appeared to from the kitchen window. That experience gave me a new respect for her routine and made the vegetables she served later taste even better.

questions.q: Describe an ambition you have not yet achieved
questions.answer:
One ambition I haven't achieved yet is to study abroad and use that opportunity to become more independent. I am still working out exactly which programme would suit me, but the goal has been on my mind for some time. It isn't simply about travelling; I want to learn in a different environment and bring useful skills back with me.

For now, the most concrete step is to **improve my English**. I have also begun to **research possible courses** and think about what I could include in a portfolio. Some days the process feels exciting; on others, the number of decisions makes it seem distant. When that happens, I try to **break the goal down** into things I can do this week, such as reading a passage, practising speaking or finishing a small project. questions.q: Describe a story you remember well
questions.answer:
A story I remember clearly is *The Lion and the Mouse*. I heard it from a family member when I was little, and years later I read it again in English. Even though I already knew the ending, I noticed details that had escaped me as a child.

The plot begins when a lion catches a mouse. Instead of eating it, he **lets the mouse go**, and the mouse promises to repay him. That seems almost comical until the lion is caught in a hunter's net. Hearing him roar, the mouse returns and **gnaws through the ropes**. It is a neat **twist in the story**: the small creature has exactly the skill the powerful one lacks. When I first heard it, I was mostly pleased that the mouse **came to the rescue**. Now I also notice the lion's decision to show mercy before he expected anything in return.

The story has **stayed with me** because it makes its point without a long explanation. It warns us not to **underestimate other people** or assume that strength is always physical. Whenever I retell it, I ask the listener which character they identify with; the answer often starts a **surprisingly thoughtful conversation**. To me, a good story should do more than **hold your attention** for a few minutes. It should **make you reconsider** an assumption and **leave a lasting impression**, and this one does both.

I also like that the ending changes the way you see the opening. The mouse's promise sounds unrealistic at first, so the rescue feels satisfying without being random. That neat structure is one reason I can recall the story years after hearing much longer tales.

questions.q: Describe a time someone asked for your opinion

A friend once asked me which online English course he should take. He had narrowed the choice to two, but the advertisements sounded almost identical, so he wanted a second opinion. I was pleased he trusted me, although I was careful not to act as if I knew everything about either course.

We sat down and **compared the course outlines**. One offered many recorded lessons; the other included regular speaking practice. I asked what he was actually finding difficult, and he admitted that he could understand a lesson but rarely spoke aloud. That helped us **get to the heart of the problem**. Instead of telling him to buy the more expensive option, I suggested that he **try a free lesson** and ask about feedback from a teacher. We also **looked beyond the advertising** and checked the timetable against his school commitments.

In the end he chose the course with speaking practice. Later, he said the comparison had helped him **make an informed decision**. What stayed with me was how useful it can be to **ask the right questions** rather than simply give an answer. If he hadn't clarified his goal, we might have focused on the wrong features. The experience made me more willing to **give honest feedback**, while also **acknowledging my limits**. An opinion is most helpful when you **take someone's needs into account** and leave them free to **make the final choice**.

I was also careful to tell my friend that a course could be excellent and still be unsuitable for him at that moment. His available time and confidence mattered as much as its reputation. That made the discussion feel less like choosing a winner and more like finding a good fit.

What made the teacher effective was her ability to **bring the subject to life** with a small example. I left feeling that I had learned a **transferable skill**, not just a trick for one test.

I still use the teacher's question in my head: what exactly in the passage supports this answer? It slows me down for a moment, but it prevents guesses based on familiar words alone. A lesson that changes my approach months later is one I consider genuinely valuable.

I went home feeling both disappointed and proud: disappointed that nerves had affected me, but proud that I had **stepped outside my comfort zone**. questions.q: Describe a time you helped a child
questions.answer:
Last summer I helped a younger relative prepare a short English presentation for school. She had written several sentences but felt nervous about saying them aloud. I didn't want to take over the assignment; my goal was to help her feel capable of doing it herself.

First, I asked her to **explain the main idea** in her own words. We then **broke the task into steps**: an opening, two examples and a final sentence. Whenever she forgot a word, I encouraged her to **use a simpler expression** instead of stopping completely. We practised in short rounds, and I **gave gentle feedback** about speaking clearly. After a while she began to **find her own voice** rather than repeat my version.

On the day of the presentation, she told me she had been nervous but had finished it. That was a relief, and I was pleased to see her **gain confidence**. The experience reminded me that helping a child doesn't always mean providing an answer. Sometimes you need to **listen with patience** and give them space to work things out. I also learned to **keep explanations simple** rather than show off what I know. If she asks for help again, I would be glad to **make time for her**. Watching her **make progress** felt more rewarding than correcting every small mistake myself.

A few weeks later, she showed me the note her teacher had written on the presentation. It praised the clarity of her explanation, not her use of difficult words. She seemed especially proud because the ideas were her own. That felt like a better result than a perfect speech written by someone else.

What I find impressive is his willingness to **start before feeling ready**. He asks questions when necessary, but he can also **work things out independently**. His progress shows that self-study is possible when you **practise regularly** and **stay curious**, even if the results are slow at first.

He also knows when to ask for help. After spending an hour stuck on a single error, he will explain what he tried and ask a more experienced person for a hint. To me, independent learning means taking initiative, not refusing every form of guidance.

My ideal job would involve building useful educational websites. I am still a student, so I know my understanding of the field is incomplete. Nevertheless, I can imagine enjoying work that combines problem-solving, design and helping other people learn.

I would like to **work on meaningful projects** with a team that listens to learners. For example, we might build a practice platform that gives clear feedback rather than just marking an answer wrong. My role could involve **turning ideas into features**, testing a page with real users and **improving it over time**. I would enjoy the challenge of making a complicated process **easy to use** without hiding important information. A good working day would end with a small improvement that someone actually notices.

I would also want a job that lets me **keep learning**. Technology changes, and I wouldn't want to rely only on what I already know. At the same time, the ideal job should allow a **healthy work-life balance**, because constant exhaustion helps nobody. I am aware that even a dream role comes with routine tasks and deadlines. If I could **handle constructive criticism**, **collaborate with others** and **see the impact of my work**, I think the difficult parts would be worth it.

If I had the choice, I'd also want to **measure success by usefulness**, not only by the number of features released. A simpler page that genuinely helps learners would make me prouder than a complicated one nobody can navigate. That value would guide the decisions I make at work.

title: Special day out that did not cost much

questions.q: Describe a cheap special day
questions.answer:
A special day out that cost very little was a walk and picnic with two friends after a demanding period of study. None of us wanted to spend much money, so we chose a park within walking distance and brought snacks from home. We didn't have an ambitious plan; we just wanted to see one another without a deadline hanging over us.

We arrived in the afternoon, found a quiet place under a tree and **shared a simple meal**. After that we **walked around the park** and talked about everything from exam questions to childhood games. At one point the weather changed and we thought it might rain, but the clouds passed. We took a few photographs, though I remember the conversations more clearly than the pictures. One friend had brought a card game, so we ended up **laughing at our mistakes** and **losing track of time**.

What made the day special was the chance to **switch off for a while** and **enjoy each other's company**. Because we had not paid for an expensive attraction, we felt no pressure to squeeze value out of every minute. I came home with a **clearer head** and a better mood. The day reminded me that you can **make good memories** on a **small budget** if the company is right. I would gladly **do it again** when we all have a free afternoon.

One friend later said it was the first afternoon in weeks when he had stopped thinking about deadlines. That comment stayed with me. I had assumed everyone needed an exciting activity to relax, but sometimes what we really need is unhurried company and a place to sit outside.

questions.q: Describe positive feedback you received about your work
questions.answer:
I once received positive feedback from an English teacher after submitting an essay. I had spent more time than usual planning it, partly because my previous attempts had wandered away from the main question. This time I wanted each paragraph to support one clear idea.

When the teacher returned it, she said my argument was easier to follow and that I had **supported my points with examples**. She also noticed that I had **used transitions naturally** rather than adding impressive-looking phrases everywhere. I felt pleased because she had commented on a specific improvement, not just written “good job” at the top. She did point out a few awkward sentences, which gave me something concrete to **work on next**.

That feedback **gave me a confidence boost**, but it also changed how I revised. I began to **read my work aloud** and ask whether a reader could **follow the line of argument**. If a sentence sounded clever but didn't help the paragraph, I cut it. The experience taught me to **value specific feedback** and **notice small improvements**. I still make mistakes, of course, yet I now know that steady practice can **pay off over time**. Hearing that from someone whose judgement I trust made the progress feel real.

The teacher's comments were especially helpful because she compared the essay with an earlier piece of mine. That showed progress I might otherwise have missed. It motivated me to **keep previous drafts** so I can see how my writing changes over time instead of judging it from a single result.

questions.q: Describe losing something in a public place
questions.answer:
I once misplaced my wallet in a bookshop after looking through a stack of books. I only realised it was missing when I reached the counter to pay. For a few seconds I felt a rush of panic because my cards and a little cash were inside.

I tried to **stay calm** and **retrace my steps** rather than search randomly. First I checked the shelf where I had put down several books, then the table near the entrance. A shop assistant noticed my expression and asked what was wrong. After I described the wallet, she checked behind the counter: another customer had **handed it in**. Nothing was missing. I was so relieved that I nearly forgot to thank her properly, but I went back and **expressed my gratitude**.

The whole incident lasted perhaps fifteen minutes, but it felt longer. It reminded me how quickly a normal outing can **turn into a stressful situation**. I was also struck by the stranger's honesty; they could have walked away, but instead **did the right thing**. Since then, I try to **keep my belongings in one place** and check my pockets before leaving a shop. If I ever find something myself, I would **return it to the staff**. That day ended well, but it taught me to **pay closer attention** in busy public places.

I also **checked the contents carefully** as soon as I got home, even though nothing seemed to be missing. It was a sensible precaution and helped me relax. Since then I have been more careful when putting something down “just for a second”, because that is often when I forget it.

questions.q: Describe a time you could not use your phone
questions.answer:
One time I was not allowed to use my phone was during a practice exam at a learning centre. Before it began, the teacher asked everyone to switch their phones off and place them in a box at the front. The rule made sense, but I was surprised by how often I reached for a device that was no longer there.

At first I felt slightly restless because I couldn't **check the time** on my screen. Then I noticed the clock on the wall and began to **focus on the task at hand**. With no notifications, I read the questions more carefully and **worked at a steady pace**. During the short break, we had to leave our phones where they were, so I **struck up a conversation** with another student instead of scrolling. We compared how we managed difficult questions without revealing answers.

After the exam, I realised the restriction had **made a noticeable difference**. I hadn't been interrupted once, and the break felt more refreshing than usual. That doesn't mean phones are bad; mine is useful for learning and staying in touch. But there are situations where **putting it away** helps me **stay present**. Since then, I sometimes **turn off notifications** when I study and **set a clear time limit** for checking messages. It is a small habit, but it can **protect my concentration**.

Interestingly, I remembered more of the break-time conversation than I would have remembered from scrolling. We talked about how nervous we felt, and that made the room seem friendlier. Losing access to my phone for a short period had unexpectedly made it easier to connect with someone nearby.

questions.q: Describe a technical problem you faced
questions.answer:
A technical problem I faced happened while I was preparing a small website for a personal project. The page looked fine on my laptop, but when I opened it on a phone, the text spilled off the screen and some buttons were impossible to tap. I had planned to show it to a friend that evening, so the timing was frustrating.

My first instinct was to **change several things at once**, which only made the problem harder to understand. I stopped, **went back to the last working version** and tested one change at a time. Eventually I realised that a fixed width in the layout was preventing the page from adjusting to a smaller screen. Once I removed it and changed the spacing, the page became **much easier to use**. I asked my friend to test it on another phone and **give honest feedback**. He noticed one more button I had missed.

Although the issue seemed minor, it taught me to **test across devices** before saying a page is finished. I also learned to **keep a backup copy** and **solve one problem at a time**. Had I continued making random changes, I might have lost the entire afternoon. Instead, I managed to **track down the cause** and **fix the layout**. The experience was annoying at the time, but it gave me more confidence in my ability to troubleshoot.

I **wrote down the cause** afterwards so I wouldn't repeat the same error in my next project. That note included the screen size that exposed the problem and the change that solved it. A record like that is much more useful than vaguely remembering that something once looked wrong.

questions.q: Describe an important use of your phone
questions.answer:
I once used my phone for something important when a relative needed directions to a clinic in an unfamiliar part of town. We had an appointment time, and the address in the message was incomplete. My phone became useful not because it was sophisticated, but because it gave us several ways to solve the problem quickly.

First, I **looked up the address** on a map and compared it with the message we had received. I then **called the reception desk** to confirm the entrance, because the building had more than one side. While we travelled, I **followed the route** and warned the driver before a turn. When we reached the area, the map showed we were close, but the entrance was hidden behind another building. I used the number again, and the receptionist **talked us through the last turn**. We arrived in time.

The experience showed me how a phone can **bring different tools together**: maps, messages and calls worked better in combination than any one of them alone. It also reminded me to **double-check important details** rather than trust the first search result. I was glad I could **help a family member** in a practical way. Since then, when an appointment matters, I **save the contact number** and **leave extra travel time**. A charged phone is useful, but **thinking ahead** mattered just as much that day.

If the battery had died, we would have needed to ask someone nearby for directions, which is why I don't think a phone should be our only plan. I now note the clinic's name and a nearby landmark before leaving. Simple preparation makes the technology more dependable.

questions.q: Describe a time you changed your plans
questions.answer:
Last year two friends and I planned a picnic in a nearby park. We had chosen the day in advance and bought simple snacks, but the weather changed abruptly that morning. The forecast had looked clear the night before; by noon it was raining hard enough to make sitting outdoors unpleasant.

At first we considered **calling the whole thing off**, since everyone had already made time for it. Then one friend suggested meeting at his family's home, where we could play a board game and share the food. We **checked with his family**, **changed the meeting place** and let the others know. Because the new plan was simple, it didn't **create extra stress**. We spent the afternoon talking and laughing while the rain continued outside.

Looking back, I am glad we didn't insist on the original idea. We would have spent the whole time **worrying about the weather**. Instead, we **made the best of the situation** and still got to see each other. The experience taught me to **stay flexible** and ask what the real aim of a plan is. Our goal wasn't the park itself; it was to spend time together. Had we remembered that from the start, the decision would have been easy. Now I try to **keep a backup option** and not let a small change **spoil the occasion**.

A week later we did finally **have the picnic in the park**, and it was enjoyable. Still, I don't think the rainy afternoon was a failed version of that day. The two meetings were different, and the indoor one gave us a story we still laugh about.

I began by **writing down my priorities** and deciding which work required my best concentration. In the morning I **revised the essay**, checking whether each paragraph actually answered the question. After lunch I rehearsed the presentation and discovered it ran well over the time limit. I had to **cut unnecessary details** without losing the main idea. Just as I was finishing, a file failed to open on another device, so I **made a backup copy** and tested it again. By evening, I was tired enough to make simple mistakes, and I forced myself to **take a proper break** before the final check.

The next morning both tasks were ready. I wasn't delighted by every sentence, but I had **met the deadlines** and learned something about my habits. I had spent too long polishing unimportant parts early in the week, leaving the difficult work until the end. Now I try to **start demanding tasks earlier** and **leave room for problems**. That day taught me that being busy is manageable when I **focus on one thing at a time** and **ask for help when needed**.

I also learned that there is a point where more revision stops improving the work. When I was exhausted, I kept rereading one line without changing anything useful. Going to bed and checking it the next morning was a better choice than pushing on simply to feel busy.

questions.q: Describe a time you had to use your imagination
questions.answer:
I had to use my imagination when a younger relative asked me to help her create a short story for a school activity. She had chosen the title “The Door in the Garden”, but neither of us knew what should happen after someone opened it. We had an afternoon to work on it, and I wanted her ideas to remain at the centre.

We began by **brainstorming possibilities**. One door led to a castle, another to a future city, but she preferred a garden where the seasons changed every time someone walked through. I asked her to **picture the scene** and describe what the character would notice first. Soon she had **come up with a character** who was frightened of winter but curious enough to enter anyway. I helped her **build a simple plot** with a beginning, a problem and a choice. Whenever I offered an idea she disliked, we set it aside rather than force it into the story.

By the end, she had written something that genuinely sounded like her. The experience reminded me that imagination is not just about wild ideas; it also helps you **see an ordinary thing differently** and **make connections**. I enjoyed **thinking outside the box**, but my biggest challenge was to **leave space for her voice**. We both felt a **sense of achievement** when she read the finished story aloud. Since then, I have been more willing to **experiment with ideas** before judging them.

She later told me that her teacher had asked the class what happened after the last page. Her answer was different from the ending we had imagined together. I liked that: the story belonged to her, and she was confident enough to keep developing it on her own.

questions.q: Describe a TV programme you enjoy watching
questions.answer:
A programme I enjoy is *Planet Earth*, a nature documentary series. I usually watch an episode at home when I have time to pay attention rather than leaving it on in the background. The landscapes and animal behaviour are interesting in themselves, but what I value most is the way the series tells a story without making nature seem simple.

An episode might follow an animal **searching for food** through changing conditions. The camera work helps viewers **notice small details** that would be easy to miss in real life. I like the moments when the narration **provides enough context** and then lets the scene speak for itself. After watching one episode, I looked up a few unfamiliar terms because I wanted to **understand the behaviour better**. Sometimes I discuss an episode with my family, and we **compare our impressions** of the same scene.

The programme is relaxing, but it can also be unsettling when it shows how hard survival can be. That combination makes it more memorable than a series that offers only beautiful pictures. It has encouraged me to **pay closer attention** to the living things around me and to **ask questions about habitats**. I don't claim to remember every fact, but the episodes **spark my curiosity** and give me reasons to **keep learning**. I would recommend it to anyone who likes programmes that can **entertain and inform** at the same time.

I would like to watch an episode with someone who knows more about wildlife and ask what the programme leaves out. A documentary necessarily selects a few scenes from a much longer process. Remembering that helps me enjoy the storytelling while staying curious about the full picture.

She reminds me that creativity can begin with a blank page and a simple question.

questions.q: Describe a difficult decision you had to make
questions.answer:
A difficult decision I made was whether to join an extra course while I already had a demanding study schedule. The course looked useful and several friends planned to attend, so I was tempted to sign up immediately. At the same time, I knew I was struggling to finish my existing work without sacrificing sleep.

I tried to **weigh up the benefits** against the time it would take. I spoke with the teacher, looked at the timetable and **asked for honest advice** from my family. A friend pointed out that I could study the same topic independently for a while and decide later whether I needed a formal class. That gave me a **middle option** I hadn't considered. In the end I **turned down the course** for that term and used the spare hours to strengthen the subjects I was already taking.

It wasn't an exciting decision, but I felt calmer once I had made it. Had I joined simply because my friends were going, I might have **spread myself too thin**. I learned that a good opportunity can still come at the wrong time. Saying no helped me **protect my priorities** and **manage my workload**. If the course is offered again, I may reconsider when I can **give it proper attention**. For now, I am satisfied that I **made a deliberate choice** rather than allowing the fear of missing out to decide for me.

questions.answer:
A friend once asked me how to prepare for an English speaking test. He was collecting complicated phrases but found it hard to answer a simple question without stopping. I recognised the problem because I had done something similar: I had spent too much time searching for impressive words and too little time speaking aloud.

I suggested that he **start with familiar topics** and record a short answer every day. We listened to one recording together, and I asked him to **notice where he paused** rather than judge his accent. We then practised a question twice. The second answer was more natural because he **focused on one clear idea** and added a small example. I also encouraged him to **learn phrases in context**, since memorised expressions sound odd when they do not fit the question.

I didn't promise that this would produce a particular score. Instead, I told him to **track his progress** over a few weeks and ask a teacher for **specific feedback**. A few days later he said the recordings were uncomfortable to hear but useful. That reaction made me smile, because it is how I had felt too. Giving advice taught me to **share what worked for me** without assuming everyone learns identically. The most helpful thing I did was probably to **listen first** and **keep the goal realistic**.

I **checked in with him** later, but I did not demand that he follow my plan exactly. He had adapted it to his own schedule and was practising more often. Seeing that taught me that advice works best when it gives someone a starting point, not another set of obligations.

Last year I wrote a long message to a relative living in another city. We usually exchange short greetings, but she had asked how my studies were going, and I wanted to give a proper answer. I typed it on my phone one evening, then read it again before sending it because I did not want it to sound like a list of achievements.

I began by **asking how she was doing** and mentioning a family event she had missed. Then I **gave her an update** about my English practice and a small website I was trying to build. I included one difficulty too: I had been struggling to **keep a consistent routine**. She had supported me before, so it felt natural to be honest rather than pretend everything was effortless. I also sent a photograph of a place we had visited together, hoping it would **bring back a good memory**.

She replied the next day with a thoughtful message of her own. Instead of giving me a lecture, she **shared a practical suggestion** about dividing a large goal into smaller steps. Our exchange helped us **stay connected across the distance**. A phone call might have been quicker, but writing allowed me to **choose my words carefully** and let her respond when she had time. I still have the conversation saved. It reminds me that a personal message can **mean a great deal** when you **make time for someone** and **write with genuine interest**.

She later said she appreciated the photograph most because it reminded her of being with the family. I had spent more time writing about study, but that small image connected the message to a shared experience. Since then, I try to include one personal detail when I write to someone far away.

questions.q: Describe an interview with a well-known person you saw or heard
questions.answer:
An interview that stayed with me was a recorded conversation with an astronaut about living and working in space. I found it while watching educational videos, and the questions were more practical than I had expected. Instead of asking only how spectacular the view was, the interviewer asked about ordinary routines and mistakes.

The astronaut described how a team has to **follow precise procedures** while still being able to **respond to unexpected problems**. One answer concerned a task that had taken much longer than planned. I liked that she **admitted the difficulty** rather than presenting the work as effortless. The interviewer then **asked a follow-up question** about how the crew communicated, which brought out a much more useful answer than a simple yes or no. I paused the recording a few times to **take in the details**.

What made the interview engaging was the balance between expertise and an ordinary human voice. I could **picture the situation** without pretending that I had experienced it myself. It also showed me how a good interviewer can **draw out a story** by listening rather than rushing to the next question. If I were able to ask the astronaut something, I would ask how that experience changed her view of teamwork back on Earth. The interview encouraged me to **ask better questions** and **look past dramatic headlines**. Even now, I remember the calm way she explained a demanding job.

I also noticed that the interviewer let her finish an answer even when she paused to think. That patience **made the conversation feel natural** and allowed an unexpected detail to emerge. Had every answer been cut short, I probably would not remember the interview as clearly.

questions.q: Describe a speech or conversation that did not interest you
questions.answer:
I once attended a long talk at a school event about a topic I had initially expected to enjoy: planning future careers. The speaker clearly had experience, so I do not want to dismiss the subject or the person. The problem was that the talk consisted mostly of broad advice with very few examples, and the audience had little chance to ask questions.

During the first ten minutes I tried to **follow the main argument**. Then the same points began to **come up repeatedly**, and I found myself **losing concentration**. I still **listened politely** because leaving in the middle would have been disruptive. To stay engaged, I wrote down two questions I would have liked to ask: how a student might **explore a field practically** and how to decide between competing interests. Neither was addressed directly.

The experience made me realise that a valuable topic does not automatically make an interesting presentation. The speaker might have **held our attention** with a short story, a case study or time for discussion. I also learned something about myself: when I give a presentation, I should **respect the audience's time**, **use concrete examples** and avoid repeating a point simply to fill the allotted time. Although I was bored, I tried not to **judge the speaker harshly**, because public speaking is difficult. That afternoon gave me a clearer idea of how to make my own explanations more useful.

Afterwards a friend asked what I thought of the talk, and I described the parts that had not answered my questions without mocking the speaker. That helped us **give fair criticism**. I would still attend another talk on the same subject if it offered concrete examples and space for questions.

questions.answer:
On a family holiday in Samarkand, we visited a small craft workshop away from the busiest tourist area. It was not the main place on our itinerary; we went in because we saw someone working near the entrance and became curious. That unplanned visit became one of the details I remember most vividly.

Inside, an artisan showed us part of the process of making a decorative object. I was surprised by how many stages were involved before the finished piece could be **put on display**. She let us **look closely at the tools** and explained how one small mistake could change a pattern. I had expected to **browse the shelves** for five minutes, but we stayed much longer and **asked plenty of questions**. My younger relative noticed a colour combination that I had overlooked, and we ended up discussing it on the way back.

The workshop gave me a different impression of the city. Famous buildings are memorable, but meeting someone who **practises a craft** helped me **see the work behind an object**. We did not buy much; the value of the visit was the conversation and the chance to observe. If I went again, I would **set aside more time** for similar small places. They can **offer a fresh perspective** on a destination and **turn an ordinary afternoon into a memory**.

Before we left, I looked again at the finished objects and noticed details I had not seen on arrival. Understanding even a little of the process **changed the way I looked at them**. That is why I consider the workshop an interesting holiday stop rather than just a shop.

questions.q: Describe an event you really enjoyed
questions.answer:
One event I enjoyed was a reading afternoon organised by a small local bookshop. It was modest compared with a concert or a festival: perhaps a dozen people gathered to discuss a short story. I almost did not go because I thought I would have nothing interesting to say, but a friend persuaded me to join him.

At the beginning, the organiser **put everyone at ease** by asking which part of the story had surprised us. That was easier to answer than a formal literary question. I **shared my first impression**, then listened as others **offered different interpretations**. One person had noticed a detail about the ending that I had missed entirely. The discussion was lively without becoming competitive, and afterwards we **stayed for tea**. I spoke to someone who had started reading in English only recently, which reminded me how varied people's reasons for joining can be.

I enjoyed the event because it made a solitary activity feel social. It gave me a reason to **read more carefully** and the confidence to **speak up in a group**. Had I stayed home, I would probably have forgotten the story within a week. Instead, the conversation **brought it to life** and helped me **connect with other readers**. I would go to a similar event again, especially if it kept the same **welcoming atmosphere**.

The organiser also asked quieter people for their views without putting them under pressure. That **made the discussion inclusive** and prevented a few confident voices from dominating. I left thinking that a small event can be memorable when everyone feels welcome to contribute.

questions.q: Describe someone who makes things by hand or with technology
questions.answer:
A friend of mine enjoys making useful things from simple materials and experimenting with digital tools. His projects are small, but each one solves a real problem for someone he knows. I first noticed his skill when he made an adjustable book stand for his younger brother, who found it uncomfortable to study with a book lying flat on the desk.

He began by **sketching a rough design** on paper, then **measured the pieces carefully**. The first version wobbled, so he changed the angle and reinforced the base. He also used a simple computer program to **test different dimensions** before cutting new material. Watching him work, I was impressed by his willingness to **learn through trial and error**. When the stand was finally stable, he asked his brother to use it for a week and **give honest feedback**. Only then did he call the project finished.

What I admire is his ability to **turn an idea into something practical**. He doesn't pretend that every attempt succeeds, and he is happy to **start from scratch** if a design is flawed. I think that combination of patience and curiosity is more valuable than simply owning expensive equipment. He has encouraged me to **solve everyday problems creatively** and to **pay attention to the user**. If I were building something with him, I would want to learn how he decides when a product is **good enough to use**.

He later made a second stand for a friend, changing the width to fit a larger book. That showed me he was not simply repeating a design; he was listening to a different user's needs. The project was modest, but it reflected a thoughtful way of working.

questions.q: Describe a food you dislike
questions.answer:
One food I have never really enjoyed is an overly sweet fruit dessert with heavy syrup. I do not dislike fruit itself; in fact, I often eat it fresh. It is the combination of the thick syrup and a very soft texture that puts me off. I first tried the dessert at a family gathering, where everyone else seemed to enjoy it.

I took a small portion because I wanted to **give it a fair chance**. The first bite was much sweeter than I expected, and after a few mouthfuls I **lost my appetite for it**. I did not make a dramatic comment, since someone had spent time preparing it. I thanked the host and chose a little tea instead. Later, when my family asked why I had left some, I explained that I **prefer lighter flavours** and usually like fruit without additional syrup.

I am aware that **taste is personal**. My relative loves that dessert, and I would never claim it is badly made simply because it does not suit me. If it were prepared with less syrup, I might **try it again**. Until then, I would rather **choose a different dessert** or have fruit on its own. The experience taught me to **be polite about food** when someone offers it, while still being honest about my preferences. I think you can **decline a second serving** without embarrassing the cook. For me, a meal is about company as well as flavour, so I would not let one disliked dish **spoil the occasion**.

I have tried other versions of the dessert, and my reaction was similar. I can still appreciate the care involved in serving it and enjoy the rest of the meal. **Respecting other people's tastes** matters to me.

questions.q: Describe a place in nature you like
questions.answer:
There is a stretch of countryside near relatives' home that I enjoy visiting when I have the chance. It is not a famous protected area or a dramatic mountain landscape. There are fields, a line of trees and a footpath that becomes particularly pleasant in the late afternoon.

On my last visit I went there with a relative after breakfast. We **followed a narrow path** and gradually left the sound of traffic behind. I could **hear birds calling** and see how the light changed over the crops. My relative pointed out where rain had changed the soil, a detail I would have missed on my own. We stopped for a while to **take in the view** and then walked back before the day became too hot. Nothing dramatic happened, but I felt calmer for having spent time there.

What I value is the chance to **slow my pace** and **pay attention to small changes**. On a screen I often move quickly from one thing to another; outdoors, I can **clear my head** without trying to be productive. I also know the area is part of people's working lives, so I try to **respect the land** and **leave no litter behind**. If I lived nearby, I would **visit more regularly**. Even an ordinary landscape can **leave a lasting impression** when you have time to notice it.

On that walk I also noticed a small change in the weather before my relative mentioned it. The air became cooler and the light softened. Those are details I would probably miss if I were rushing to reach a landmark. The place rewards attention rather than a packed itinerary.

questions.q: Describe a journey you often make but dislike
questions.answer:
A journey I often make but do not enjoy is a crowded bus ride to a learning centre during the busiest part of the day. Most trips are perfectly manageable, and I am grateful there is a route at all. The problem is the combination of traffic, noise and uncertainty about how long the journey will take.

One afternoon stands out. I had allowed what I thought was plenty of time, but a delay meant the bus **moved at a crawl** for much of the route. The vehicle was full, so it was difficult to **find a comfortable place to stand**. I kept **checking the time**, worrying that I would miss the start of a class. When we finally got moving, the noise made it hard to concentrate on the notes I had brought. I arrived just in time, but I felt tired before the lesson had even begun.

Since then, I have tried to **leave a little earlier** and **prepare a backup route** when something important is scheduled. I also avoid expecting myself to study seriously on a crowded bus; listening to a short recording is more realistic. The journey is not a disaster, but it can **put me in a bad mood** if I let every delay frustrate me. Ideally, more predictable transport would **make daily life easier** for everyone using the route. For now, I try to **plan around the uncertainty** and **arrive with time to spare**.

One day I considered walking the last section instead of staying on the bus, but it would have taken too long before class. The experience helped me **make more realistic plans**: a route may look short on a map and still be unpredictable at a busy hour.

questions.q: Describe someone who struggled but succeeded
questions.answer:
A person I admire is an older acquaintance who had to rebuild his small tutoring business after an unexpectedly difficult year. I do not know every financial detail, so I would not present his story as a business case study. What I saw was the effort he made to keep serving students when his first plan stopped working.

He had relied mainly on in-person lessons, but circumstances changed and attendance fell. Rather than **give up on the project**, he asked students what they needed and **adapted his teaching materials**. He began with short online sessions, discovered that some students had poor connections and then created smaller downloadable exercises. He also **asked for honest feedback** instead of pretending that every change was successful. For a while he seemed exhausted, but he continued to **make steady improvements**. Gradually students returned, and his lessons became more flexible than before.

What I respect is his **willingness to change course**. Success did not come from a single brilliant idea; it came from noticing problems and responding to them. He told me once that he had learned to **take one step at a time** when the bigger picture felt overwhelming. Watching him encouraged me to **deal with setbacks** without treating them as a verdict on my ability. I cannot say his work is easy now, but he has **regained his confidence** and **kept his commitment to students**. That is the kind of success I find convincing.

I once asked him whether he wished he had started with a different plan. He said the first version had taught him what students really needed, even though it failed in some ways. That answer helped me **see failure as information** rather than just an embarrassing outcome.

A school friend of mine hopes to work in medicine, ideally as a doctor. We have known each other for several years, and I have seen how seriously she takes biology. She is also the person in our group who listens carefully when someone is worried, although I know that kindness alone is not enough for a medical career.

She first **became interested in healthcare** after accompanying a family member to a clinic. What stayed with her was how a clinician **explained each step clearly**, making a stressful visit easier to handle. Since then, my friend has **worked hard at science** and looked into the years of training involved. She knows she will have to **develop practical skills** as well as pass examinations. When we discuss the future, she speaks about caring for patients, but also about the need to **make careful decisions** when information is incomplete.

I admire her because she does not **romanticise the profession**. She understands that long hours and difficult conversations may be part of the job. If she eventually qualifies, I think her ability to **treat people with respect** will matter alongside medical knowledge. I cannot predict exactly where her studies will lead, but she is willing to **put in sustained effort**. Talking with her has reminded me that choosing a profession means learning about its **everyday responsibilities**, not only its title. I hope she gets the chance to **follow that path**.

She sometimes asks me to listen while she explains a science concept in plain language. It helps her check what she understands, and I often learn something too. I like that she shares what she learns rather than treating study as a private competition.

questions.q: Describe a time you received good service
questions.answer:
I once received excellent service in a small bookshop when I was looking for an English book that would challenge me without being frustrating. I had been browsing for a while, and a member of staff asked whether I wanted a suggestion. She did not immediately direct me to the most expensive shelf.

First she **asked about my reading level** and what kind of subjects I enjoyed. I explained that I wanted a story with language I could follow but also learn from. She showed me two options and **pointed out the differences** in length and style. Then she suggested that I **read a page from each** before deciding. That simple idea helped me notice that one book felt manageable and the other required a dictionary in almost every paragraph. She gave me time to **make up my own mind** and never made me feel rushed.

I bought the first book and later returned to thank her because I actually finished it. What made the service good was her willingness to **listen to my needs** rather than assume what I should buy. questions.q: Describe a time you saw children misbehaving
questions.answer:
I remember seeing a group of children behaving badly on a bus one afternoon. They were not doing anything dangerous, but they were shouting across the aisle and repeatedly kicking the back of another passenger's seat. The adult travelling with them seemed distracted and did not notice at first.

I initially tried to **ignore the noise**, because children can get restless on a long journey. Then the passenger in front turned round and **asked them politely** to stop kicking the seat. The children laughed, and one of them carried on. Their adult companion finally noticed and **spoke to them firmly**. She did not shout, but she explained that other people needed space too. After a few minutes they settled down, and the passenger thanked her. Watching the situation, I realised how easy it would be to **make a snap judgement** about the family without knowing whether the children were tired or upset.

The behaviour was inconsiderate, yet I think the calm response worked better than public humiliation would have. Children have to **learn social boundaries**, and adults can help by **setting clear expectations**. If I had been the passenger, I hope I could have **raised the issue respectfully**. The incident made me think about how shared spaces depend on people **taking others into account**. It also reminded me that correcting behaviour does not require **losing your temper** or **embarrassing a child**.

I also noticed that the children settled more quickly once the adult gave them something to do during the rest of the journey. That small change suggested they had been restless, not deliberately trying to upset strangers. It did not excuse the kicking, but it made the situation easier to understand.

questions.q: Describe something you do regularly but consider a waste of time
questions.answer:
A routine I consider a waste of time is checking several apps in a row when I am about to start studying. I tell myself I am only looking for an important message, but one notification leads to another. Ten minutes can pass before I have opened the book I intended to read.

I first noticed the habit when I **tracked my study sessions**. The problem was not any single app; it was the repeated decision to **pick up my phone** whenever a task felt difficult. If I didn't immediately understand a paragraph, I would **look for an easy distraction** rather than work through it. The routine gave me a false sense of being busy, even though I rarely **found anything urgent**. Once I saw the pattern, I began to **turn off notifications** and leave the phone out of reach for a short block of time.

I still need my phone for study sometimes, so simply banning it would be unrealistic. What helps is **setting a specific purpose** before I unlock it: am I checking a word or just avoiding an awkward question? If it is the latter, I try to **return to the task** for five minutes. That small change has helped me **protect my attention** without pretending I will never use social media. I would rather **make conscious choices** than let an automatic routine **eat into my time**.

I now put a piece of paper next to my desk and write down any unrelated thought that occurs while I work. That keeps me from opening an app to deal with it immediately. At the end of a study block, I can decide whether the thought was actually important.

We **agreed on a clear goal**: each of us would try a short passage independently, then explain the questions we had answered differently. That structure prevented the meeting from becoming casual conversation. When I explained my choice, a classmate **pointed out a clue** I had missed in the text. In return, I helped another student understand why a similar-looking phrase did not support her answer. We **learned from each other's mistakes** and finished the session with a clearer idea of what to practise next.

I did not suddenly decide that every group is effective. Without a goal, a study session can still **drift off topic**. But that experience made me **reconsider my assumption**. I now study alone when I need quiet concentration and **work with others** when discussion can reveal something I have overlooked. Changing my mind felt slightly uncomfortable because I had been so certain. In the end, I was glad I had **given it a fair try**. It taught me to **stay open to evidence** and **avoid judging too quickly**.

I have since used the same approach with another assumption: I first ask what evidence might change my view. That does not mean I abandon my opinion whenever someone disagrees. It means I can **test an idea fairly** rather than protect it automatically.
